stem: Which profit figure is used in the numerator of return on capital employed (ROCE)?

options.content: Profit from operations
options.rationale: Correct: it is the profit before finance costs and tax.

options.content: Profit for the year
options.rationale: That is after finance costs and tax; it is used for profit margin.

options.content: Gross profit
options.rationale: Gross profit is before the operating expenses.

options.content: Profit before tax and after interest
options.rationale: That is after finance costs, which reward the lenders whose capital is included.

explanation: ROCE = profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100. Capital employed includes the loan notes, so the profit must be before their interest.

stem: Which ratio is calculated by dividing gross profit by cost of sales?

options.content: Mark-up
options.rationale: Correct: cost of sales is the base for mark-up.

options.content: Gross profit margin
options.rationale: Margin divides gross profit by revenue.

options.content: Expenses to revenue
options.rationale: That ratio divides operating expenses by revenue.

options.content: Profit margin
options.rationale: Profit margin divides profit for the year by revenue.

explanation: Mark-up = gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100. Margin uses revenue as the base.

stem: Capital employed, as used in ROCE, is made up of:

options.content: issued shares and all reserves only
options.rationale: That is equity; it excludes the loan notes.

options.content: total assets and current liabilities
options.rationale: Current liabilities are deducted, not added.

options.content: issued shares, all reserves and non-current liabilities
options.rationale: Correct: this equals total assets less current liabilities.

options.content: non-current assets and working capital less all reserves
options.rationale: Reserves are part of the capital employed.

explanation: Capital employed = issued shares + all reserves + non-current liabilities = total assets less current liabilities.

stem: A trader adds a mark-up of 60% to cost. What is the gross profit margin on sales?

options.rationale: That is the mark-up; margin uses revenue as the base.
This subtracts the mark-up from 100 instead of dividing by 160.
This is the mark-up that goes with a 40% margin; the two ratios have been reversed.

explanation: Cost 100, profit 60, selling price 160, so the margin is 60 ÷ 160 = 37.5%.
hints: If cost is 100, the selling price is 160.

stem: Revenue and operating expenses both rose by 10%, but gross profit margin fell from 35% to 32%. What happened to the profit margin?

options.content: It rose, because the higher revenue gave the business more profit in total
options.rationale: Higher revenue helps only if the margin is kept.

options.content: It fell, because the lower margin on sales was not offset by cost control
options.rationale: Correct: expenses grew in line with revenue so the full fall in margin passed through.

options.content: It stayed the same, because expenses rose in line with revenue
options.rationale: The gross margin fell, so less profit remains from each dollar.

options.content: It cannot be judged without knowing the rate of income tax
options.rationale: A fall in gross margin with proportionate expenses lowers the profit margin whatever the tax.

explanation: With expenses to revenue unchanged, a fall of three percentage points in gross margin lowers the profit margin by the same amount before tax.
hints: Expenses to revenue stayed the same, so only the gross margin changed.

stem: Which change would most directly improve a company's gross profit margin?

options.content: Reducing the salaries of the administration staff and office costs
options.rationale: Administrative expenses are below gross profit.

options.content: Repaying part of the loan notes from the bank balance
options.rationale: That affects finance costs, which are below gross profit.

options.content: Buying inventory from a cheaper supplier at the same quality
options.rationale: Correct: a lower cost of sales raises gross profit for the same revenue.

options.content: Selling surplus land to raise cash for the business
options.rationale: A sale of land does not change the cost of goods sold.

explanation: Gross margin depends on the selling price and the cost of goods sold; the other changes affect expenses or finance, which are deducted later.
hints: Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales only.

stem: At the year end a company raises new loan notes and holds the cash unspent. Profit from operations is unchanged. What happens to ROCE?

options.content: It rises, because the company has more cash
options.rationale: Cash does not add to operating profit.

options.content: It is unchanged, because profit from operations is unchanged
options.rationale: The denominator has increased.

options.content: It rises, because loan notes are cheaper than shares
options.rationale: The cost of finance is not part of ROCE.

options.content: It falls, because capital employed increases
options.rationale: Correct: the numerator is unchanged and the denominator rises.

explanation: Loan notes are part of capital employed. With the same profit from operations a larger base gives a lower return.

stem: Two bakeries have the same ROCE. Bakery P has a high margin and slow capital turnover; Bakery Q has a low margin and fast capital turnover. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Bakery P must be better managed
options.rationale: Equal ROCE shows equal overall return; management quality is not shown.

options.content: Both can earn the same return by different routes
options.rationale: Correct: ROCE = margin × capital turnover.

options.content: Bakery Q must have lower costs
options.rationale: A low margin does not prove lower costs.

options.content: The ratios cannot be equal when the margins differ
options.rationale: Different margins can be offset by different turnover.

explanation: A high margin with slow turnover and a low margin with fast turnover can give the same ROCE.
hints: Think of ROCE as margin multiplied by turnover.

stem: A mark-up of 50% on cost is the same as a gross profit margin of 50% on sales.
explanation: False. A mark-up of 50% gives a margin of 50 ÷ 150 = 33.3%.

stem: ROCE can fall in a year when profit from operations rises.
explanation: True. If capital employed rises faster than profit from operations, ROCE falls.

stem: Match each ratio to its formula.
explanation: Margins use revenue as the base, mark-up uses cost of sales and ROCE uses the capital employed.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Gross profit margin is calculated as gross profit divided by {{blank:a}}. Expenses to revenue shows the control of {{blank:b}} costs.

explanation: Gross profit margin uses revenue as the base; expenses to revenue measures distribution and administrative expenses against revenue.

stem: Name the ratio calculated as profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100.
explanation: It is return on capital employed (ROCE).

stem: A company's revenue was US\$241,500 and its cost of sales was US\$169,050. Calculate the gross profit margin as a percentage to one decimal place.
explanation: Gross profit = 241,500 - 169,050 = 72,450. Margin = 72,450 ÷ 241,500 × 100 = 30.0%. Using cost of sales as the base would give the mark-up of 42.9%.
workedSolution: 1. Gross profit = 241,500 - 169,050 = 72,450. Margin = 72,450 ÷ 241,500 × 100 = 30.0%. Using cost of sales as the base would give the mark-up of 42.9%.

stem: At 31 December 2025 a company had issued share capital of US\$70,000, retained earnings of US\$69,550 and loan notes of US\$62,000. Its profit from operations for the year was US\$33,250 and its profit for the year was US\$23,550. Calculate ROCE as a percentage to one decimal place.
explanation: Capital employed = 70,000 + 69,550 + 62,000 = 201,550. ROCE = 33,250 ÷ 201,550 × 100 = 16.5%. Dividing by equity alone or using profit for the year are the usual errors.
workedSolution: 1. Capital employed = 70,000 + 69,550 + 62,000 = 201,550. ROCE = 33,250 ÷ 201,550 × 100 = 16.5%. Dividing by equity alone or using profit for the year are the usual errors.
hints: Capital employed includes the loan notes.
Use profit before finance costs and tax.

stem: A shop marks up all goods by 40% on cost. Calculate the gross profit margin as a percentage to one decimal place.
explanation: Cost 100, selling price 140, profit 40. Margin = 40 ÷ 140 × 100 = 28.6%. The mark-up (40%) uses cost as the base.
workedSolution: 1. Cost 100, selling price 140, profit 40. Margin = 40 ÷ 140 × 100 = 28.6%. The mark-up (40%) uses cost as the base.

stem: ZIMSEC style. Return on equity = profit for the year ÷ equity × 100. A company's profit for the year was US\$23,550 and its equity was US\$139,550. Calculate return on equity as a percentage to one decimal place.
explanation: 23,550 ÷ 139,550 × 100 = 16.9%. Dividing by total assets would give return on assets.
workedSolution: 1. 23,550 ÷ 139,550 × 100 = 16.9%. Dividing by total assets would give return on assets.
hints: Equity is shares plus all reserves.

stem: Explain why ROCE uses profit from operations and not profit for the year.

points.description: Capital employed includes the non-current liabilities, whose lenders are paid through finance costs
So the profit must be before finance costs (and tax) to give a fair return on all the capital

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Capital employed includes loan notes. The lenders' reward is the interest, so profit is taken before finance costs to match the capital it is compared with.

explanation: One mark for the loan notes being in capital employed and one for profit before interest matching it.

stem: A trader's gross profit margin fell from 38.0% to 34.0% while revenue rose by 15%. Suggest two possible reasons and comment on whether the higher revenue was worthwhile.

points.description: Reason 1: the selling price was reduced (discounts) to win sales
Reason 2: the cost of goods or ingredients rose and was not passed on, or the sales mix moved to low-margin items
Gross profit rose by much less than revenue (about 2.9% against 15%)
Judgement: the extra sales were worthwhile only if the extra gross profit exceeded the extra expenses

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A price cut to win customers or dearer goods could explain the lower margin. Gross profit rose by only about 2.9% on revenue growth of 15%, so each extra dollar of sales earned less. The growth was worthwhile only if the extra gross profit covered the extra expenses.

explanation: Two marks for reasons, one for the comparison of growth rates and one for a judgement.
hints: Link each reason to the margin, not to revenue.

stem: The directors of Kadoma Cables Ltd note that ROCE fell from 25.7% in 2024 to 16.5% in 2025 although revenue rose. Use the figures to explain the fall: revenue 218,000 to 241,500; gross profit margin 35.0% to 30.0%; capital employed 155,000 to 201,550.

points.description: The gross profit margin fell from 35.0% to 30.0%
Profit from operations fell from 39,800 to 33,250 although revenue rose
Capital employed increased from 155,000 to 201,550
A lower numerator over a larger denominator lowers ROCE
Conclusion: the new capital (loan notes) has not yet earned a return; the directors should restore the margin

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Revenue rose but the gross margin fell, so profit from operations fell from 39,800 to 33,250. At the same time capital employed rose to 201,550 because of extra loan notes. A smaller profit over a bigger base gives the lower ROCE; the directors should restore the margin.

explanation: One mark each for the margin, the fall in profit from operations, the rise in capital, the effect on the fraction and the conclusion.
hints: Treat ROCE as a fraction: what happened to the top and to the bottom?

parts.stem: Evaluate the profitability of the two businesses and advise a bank which should receive a loan for expansion. Use your calculations.

points.description: Masvingo has the higher gross margin (35.0% against 20.0%)
Bulawayo spends a lower share of revenue on expenses (11.4% against 14.3%)
Bulawayo's low margin suggests a high-volume, low-price strategy
ROCE: 23.1% for Bulawayo and 24.9% for Masvingo
Identifies the business with the better ROCE and links it to margin and capital
Notes that Masvingo has more loan notes already, so more finance cost and risk
Recommends one business with a reason

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Masvingo earns the higher gross margin (35.0%) but spends more of its revenue on expenses. ROCE is 24.9% against 23.1% for Bulawayo, so Masvingo gives the better return on its capital although it already carries more loan notes. On profitability alone Masvingo is the better borrower, but one year's figures are not enough; the bank should also consider cash flow, security and the quality of management.
